In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of biofilm development in response to bacteriophage exposure.
the interaction of phages and bacteria, and in particular the effect of phages on biofilms.
phage resistance development in biofilm populations, and the role of phage-encoded toxins in the context of biofilm formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phages are capable of inducing a rapid conversion of biofilm populations, either into lysogens or resistant bacteria.
the dynamics within structured biofilms are highly dependent on the type of phage used and the phages’ mode of action.
phage exposure of biofilms can lead to either rapid lysogenization or rapid resistance development, depending on the nature of the phage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phages can have a major impact on bacterial biofilms, and that the outcome of this interaction can be very different, depending on the phage type.
phages can be used to manipulate biofilm populations, and that the phage-bacteria interactions within a biofilm are more complex than those observed in a liquid culture.
phages can rapidly lead to a shift in the population dynamics within structured bacterial communities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phage-bacterium interactions are not limited to the single cell level, but also include the community level.
the dynamics within structured populations of bacterial cells can be strongly affected by a single dose of phage.
the phage exposure history of a bacterial population is a crucial determinant of the outcome of phage-bacteria interactions.
